introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá returned again and again, in talks across Europe and America and in letters, to one diagnosis: prejudice of race, religion, nation, politics and class is the cause of war and the destroyer of human society, and its removal is a religious duty. The readings repeat the list many times; the later ones ask the Bahá’ís to be known as people without prejudice, and letters written after them admit that they are not yet free of it. Beside them stand the scriptures' own words on the stranger, the Samaritan and the unclean, with Shylock, Montaigne, Twain and Douglass. Contrasts come from Du Bois and Blackmun on race, from Burke, who thought some prejudices worth keeping, and from those who doubt that prejudice alone explains war.
questions: The readings name religious, racial, national, political and economic prejudice together. Are these one thing, or do they need different remedies?
Burke defends inherited prejudice and the little platoon. What would the readings keep of what he praises, and what would they remove?
Several readings say the Bahá’ís have no prejudices; a later letter says they are tainted with it, perhaps unconsciously. How should a community hold both statements?
Is every war caused by prejudice? What would Thucydides or Marx add?
What does it take, in practice, to visit the church, mosque or home one was taught to avoid?

outside.why: Samuel is told that man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart.
Malachi asks whether we have not all one father, and why then we deal treacherously with one another.
James asks every man to be swift to hear, slow to speak and slow to wrath.
The Qur’an counts the difference of languages and colours among the signs of God.
Booker T. Washington proposed separation in things social and unity in mutual progress. If colour is the one point of distinction, how much of life may it still be allowed to govern?
Du Bois describes the twoness of an American and a Negro in one dark body. Can one who has not lived it say that colour is only one small distinction?
Paul tells the Athenians that God made of one blood all nations of men.
Shylock asks whether a Jew has not eyes, hands, senses, affections, as a Christian has.
The Mishnah says a single person was created first so that none could say, my father was greater than yours.
Justice Blackmun held that to get beyond racism we must first take account of race. Is it enough to call colour a strange ground of strife, or must its history be reckoned with?
Peter perceives that God is no respecter of persons, but accepts those in every nation who fear him.
Bacon observed that the understanding is no dry light, but takes an infusion from the will and affections.
Kant found the root of tutelage in the want of courage to use one's own understanding.
Burke defends the English for cherishing their old prejudices, and because they are prejudices. Is all inherited feeling for one's own a breeding-ground of tragedy?
The Qur’an records the answer of every people to its messenger: we follow that wherein we found our fathers.
Jesus asks why we see the mote in a brother's eye and miss the beam in our own.
Proverbs gives the rule of fairness: the first to plead seems just until his neighbour searches him.
Swift remarked that we have just enough religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another.
The Qur’an reports the claim that none enters paradise but a Jew or a Christian, and asks for the proof.
Pascal noted that men never do evil so completely and cheerfully as when they do it from religious conviction.
Peter is told in a vision that what God has cleansed he must not call common or unclean.
The woman at the well is astonished to be asked for water, for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.
In the parable it is the despised Samaritan who has compassion on the wounded stranger.
Jesus tells of a publican who would not lift his eyes to heaven and asked only for mercy, the reverse of dogmatic superiority.
Mill holds that he who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that. How would the community described here describe itself?
Montaigne found nothing barbarous in a distant nation except that everyone calls barbarism what is not his own custom.
The Qur’an says there is no compulsion in religion; the right direction is distinct from error.
When disciples would call down fire on a village of another faith, Jesus rebukes them.
Jesus tells John not to forbid one who does good outside their company.
Garrison took as his motto that our country is the world and our countrymen are mankind.
James traces wars and fightings to the lusts that war in our members.
The Athenians tell the Melians that the strong do what they can. Is every war caused by prejudice, or do interest and fear make wars among people who think well of each other?
Kipling's ballad begins with East and West that shall never meet, and goes on to two strong men who do.
Burke calls love of the little platoon the first link toward love of country and mankind. Is patriotic feeling a prejudice to remove or an affection to widen?
Diogenes, asked where he came from, said he was a citizen of the world.
William James observed that showing war's irrationality and horror has no effect on those drawn to it. If prejudice were gone, would the appetite for war go with it?
An Upanishad calls mine-and-theirs the reckoning of the narrow-minded; to the noble the world is one family.
Zamenhof held difference of speech to be a first cause of antipathy between peoples.
Marx told the workers they had nothing to lose but their chains. Is class division a prejudice to be given up, or an interest to be settled?
UNESCO's founders concluded that wars begin in the minds of men, and there the defences of peace must be built.
Jesus says that every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and no house so divided shall stand.
Ashoka held that contact between religions is good, and that one should listen to the doctrines of others.
Adam Smith observed that we address ourselves to the self-love of the butcher and the baker. Is commercial rivalry a prejudice, or the ordinary working of trade?
King wrote that we are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality: injustice anywhere threatens justice everywhere.
Arnold sees a darkling plain swept with confused alarms, where ignorant armies clash by night.
Isaiah says that the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.
The psalm exclaims how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
Haile Selassie told the nations that until the philosophy of superior and inferior races is abandoned, peace will be an illusion.
Paul says there is neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female.
John's letter says that whoever claims to love God and hates his brother is a liar.
The Universal Declaration begins that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
John Ball asked the peasants: when Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?
Paul says the middle wall of partition between peoples has been broken down.
The Qur’an says mankind was made nations and tribes that they may know one another, the noblest being the best in conduct.
Paul's rule for inquiry: prove all things, hold fast that which is good.
Tennyson looked to a parliament of man and a federation of the world.
Isaiah has God invite his people: come now, and let us reason together.
Isaiah foresees strangers made joyful in a house of prayer for all people.
Jesus blesses the peacemakers, who shall be called the children of God.
Jesus calls his hearers the light of the world and asks that their light be seen.
Jesus says that whoever would be chiefest shall be servant of all.
The Dhammapada says a man is not a Brahmana by his family or birth, but by truth and righteousness.
Heschel held that no religion is an island: we are all involved with one another.
Acts shows Parthians, Medes, Elamites and strangers of Rome gathered and hearing together.
Paul thanks God upon every remembrance of his friends, for their fellowship.
Jesus says that all shall know his disciples by their love one for another.
Saadi calls the children of Adam limbs of one another, and denies the name of human to one untroubled by another's pain.
Kennedy named the common link: we all inhabit this small planet and breathe the same air.
James tells any who lack wisdom to ask of God, who gives to all liberally.
Wilson proposed a general association of nations with guarantees for great and small alike.
Jesus sums up the law in love of God and love of neighbour.
Jesus says that people are known by their fruits, which is what the newspapers are asked to report.
Penn thought the humble, meek, merciful and just are everywhere of one religion.
Jesus asks that good works be seen so that God is glorified.
Peter asks believers to give a reason for their hope with meekness.
Plato's prisoners take the shadows on the wall for the whole of reality.
Malachi promises that the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings.
Goethe said that a man with no acquaintance with foreign languages knows nothing of his own.
Paul hears the whole creation groaning and travailing together, as before a birth.
Tocqueville noted that Americans of all conditions constantly form associations for every purpose.
Paul asks believers not to be conformed to this world but transformed by the renewing of the mind.
The Qur’an forbids one folk to deride another, who may be better than they.
Twain held that travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, which need it sorely.
Leviticus commands that the stranger be as one born among you, and loved as thyself.
The Qur’an has believers say that they make no distinction between any of God's messengers.
Darwin expected sympathy to extend as small tribes unite into larger communities. Is prejudice removed by teaching, or outgrown as communities enlarge?
The psalmist says the Lord is on his side, and asks what man can do unto him.
Zechariah names the power meant: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
Jesus says the Father makes his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.
Francis praises God through brother sun, brother wind and sister water, kin to all that is made.
Paul tells converts that they are no more strangers and foreigners but fellow citizens.
Peter says God has shown him that he should not call any man common or unclean.
Franklin admitted that had he overcome pride he would probably be proud of his humility. What happens to a virtue when a community announces that it has it?
John's letter says that if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. Can any community say of itself that it has no prejudice?
Paul asks each not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think.
James forbids his assembly to seat the man with the gold ring above the poor man in vile raiment.
Exodus forbids oppressing the stranger, for ye know the heart of a stranger.
Burns will not have honest poverty hang its head, and passes by the coward-slave who is ashamed of it.
Douglass held that if there is no struggle there is no progress.
Jeremiah calls the heart deceitful above all things, and asks who can know it.
